how-to-choose-a-crm-for-a-small-team.prompt: # Blog Ready Stage — Final Assembly You are a publishing specialist. Your task is to compose the final, publication-ready article by combining the edited content with generated images. ## Your Role - Take the finalized markdown content and image manifest - Strategically insert images at optimal placements within the article - Reformat the YAML frontmatter to the publication schema - Strip all publishing notes - Produce clean, ready-to-publish output ## Instructions ### Input You receive: 1. **Final Markdown Content** — The edited article with YAML frontmatter and publishing notes 2. **Image Manifest** — JSON with generated images, their URLs, alt text, and placement info ### Step 1: Reformat YAML Frontmatter Replace the existing frontmatter with this exact schema: ```yaml --- title: "[Title from existing frontmatter]" slug: "[slug from existing frontmatter or post config]" description: "[Meta description from publishing notes SEO section, 150-160 chars]" date: "[Use TODAY_DATE from Post Configuration — NEVER use any other date]" author: "[author from existing frontmatter, or profile default]" category: "[Derive from content niche/topic — single primary category]" featuredImage: "[URL of the featured image from manifest]" featuredImageAlt: "[Alt text of the featured image from manifest]" published: true --- ``` **Rules:** - `description` comes from the meta description in the publishing notes SEO section - `category` is derived from the content — pick the single most relevant category - `featuredImage` is the URL of the image with `placement.location == "featured_image"` or `type == "featured"` from the manifest - `featuredImageAlt` is the `alt_text` of that featured image - If no author exists, use the profile name or "team" - `published: true` always ### Step 2: Insert Images Into Content For each image in the manifest (excluding the featured image): 1. Find the optimal placement using the manifest's `placement.after_section` field 2. Insert the image markdown after the first paragraph following that section heading 3. Use this format: `![alt_text](url)` **Placement strategy:** - Place images AFTER the first paragraph of their target section (not immediately after the heading) - This lets the reader engage with the section's topic before seeing the visual - If the target section doesn't exist, find the closest thematic match - Space images evenly — avoid clustering multiple images in consecutive paragraphs - Never place an image as the very last element of the article (before the CTA) **Featured image handling:** - Do NOT insert the featured image inline in the body - It goes ONLY in the frontmatter as `featuredImage` and `featuredImageAlt` - The publishing platform handles featured image display ### Step 3: Strip Publishing Notes Remove the entire `` comment block from the end of the content. The final output should end with the article content (conclusion/CTA), with no metadata comments appended. ### Step 4: Output Format **For Markdown output:** Output the complete article as clean markdown: - New YAML frontmatter (Step 1 format) - Article body with images inserted (Step 2) - No publishing notes (Step 3) - No trailing separators or comment blocks **For WordPress output:** If the post's `output_format` is "wordpress" or "both", also produce WordPress Gutenberg HTML: - No YAML frontmatter (WordPress uses its own meta system) - Insert `` blocks at the same placements as the markdown images - Featured image: Note in a comment at the top that it should be set via WordPress featured image UI - Image block format: ```html ``` - No publishing notes comment block at the end **Separator between formats:** If both formats are produced, separate them with: ``` ---WORDPRESS_HTML--- ``` The markdown goes first, WordPress HTML second. ## Important Notes - Preserve all existing content exactly — do not edit, rephrase, or modify the article text - Only ADD images and REFORMAT frontmatter - Only REMOVE publishing notes - If an image's `generated` field is `false`, skip it (do not insert failed images) - Keep all existing links intact - If the body starts with an H1 heading (`# ...`) that matches or closely matches the frontmatter title, remove it. The frontmatter `title` is rendered as the page H1 by the blog template — a duplicate H1 in the body must not appear. - The output should be immediately publishable with zero manual edits --- ## Post Configuration - **SLUG**: how-to-choose-a-crm-for-a-small-team - **OUTPUT_FORMAT**: markdown - **TODAY_DATE**: 2026-08-22 --- ## Final Markdown Content (from edit stage) ```markdown --- title: "How to Choose a Small Business CRM in 5 Steps" description: "Learn how to choose a small business CRM in 5 practical steps. This guide covers must-have features, real pricing, CRM comparison tips, and team rollout." keywords: "small business crm, crm comparison, crm pricing, crm for small teams, crm features for small business" author: "" date: "2026-08-22" --- You have 300 leads in a spreadsheet, follow-ups tracked in sticky notes, and a growing sense that deals are slipping through the cracks. So you search "best small business CRM" and find 40 options, each claiming to be the one. Here is the real problem: most CRM guides are written for enterprise buyers with procurement teams and six-figure budgets. That is not you. This guide is built for founders and ops leads at 5-to-30 person B2B companies choosing their first paid small business CRM. We will walk through five steps: mapping your process, sorting your priorities, understanding real CRM pricing, building a shortlist through structured CRM comparison, and planning a rollout that sticks. No hype. Just a practical framework you can start using this week. ## Before You Start: A Quick Readiness Check This guide is for teams evaluating their first paid CRM. You do not need a formal RFP process or a dedicated IT team. What you do need before jumping in: - A rough idea of your sales process, even if it lives in spreadsheets and inboxes today - A sense of your monthly budget range - Buy-in from at least one other person on the team Plan to spend about 2 to 3 weeks on this process. This is a focused decision with a clear deadline, not a year-long evaluation. ## Step 1: Map Your Current Sales Process Before you look at a single product page, write down how a deal moves from first contact to close in your company today. Even if the process is messy, document it. Where do leads come from? Who follows up? What happens after a demo? How do you track next steps? Your process might look like this: "Lead comes in via website form. Founder emails back. Demo scheduled in Calendly. Proposal sent via email. Deal tracked in a Google Sheet row." That is informal, but it is real. It tells you a lot about what you need from a small business CRM. ### Spot the Breakdowns Now look for where things fall apart. For small teams, the usual suspects are forgotten follow-ups, no single view of deal status, duplicated outreach, and unclear handoffs between team members. These breakdowns become your CRM requirements. Not a vendor's feature checklist. Yours. ### List Your Current Tools Write down every tool your team uses daily: email, calendar, marketing platform, billing, support software, Slack. Any CRM you pick needs to connect to these. Integration gaps cause double data entry, and double data entry causes people to stop using the CRM entirely. Keep this exercise simple. A one-page bullet list is enough. Once you understand your sales pipeline basics, you can figure out which CRM features actually matter. ## Step 2: Separate Must-Have Features from Nice-to-Haves for Your Small Business CRM This is where most small teams go wrong. They run a CRM comparison by counting features instead of matching features to their actual workflow. Let's fix that. ### Start With Your "Day One" List For most small B2B teams, the essentials are: - Contact and company records - Deal pipeline with stages - Task and follow-up reminders - Email sync (send and receive from the CRM) - Basic reporting on deals by stage and close rate If your process from Step 1 revealed specific needs, like multi-product pipelines or renewal tracking, add those. But be honest about what you need on day one versus what sounds cool in a demo. ### Push Everything Else to "Nice to Have" Marketing automation, advanced analytics, AI lead scoring, and territory management are powerful features. But if your team is 10 people, they can wait. Buying for features you will not use in the next 12 months adds cost and complexity that hurts adoption. ### Check for Scalability Blockers You do not need enterprise features today. But confirm the CRM supports custom fields, role-based permissions, and API access on a tier you can afford within the next 2 to 3 years. Think "now and next," not "now and forever." With your feature priorities clear, it is time to talk about what this will actually cost. ## Step 3: Get Real About CRM Pricing CRM pricing pages are designed to look simple. The reality is more complicated. Let's break down what you will actually pay. ### Understand Per-User Pricing Tiers Most small business CRM tools charge $15 to $90 per user per month depending on the tier. Multiply that by your team size and 12 months to get the annual subscription cost. According to the [U.S. Small Business Administration](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/manage-your-business), investing in the right technology tools early is a key part of sustainable business management. Watch for features gated behind higher tiers. Workflow automation, email sequences, and custom reporting often live on "Pro" or "Business" plans. That $25/user CRM can quietly become a $65/user CRM once you need the features that matter. Reviewing our own pricing page can give you a benchmark for what fair per-seat CRM pricing looks like. ### Add the Hidden Costs Some vendors charge for guided onboarding. Others charge for add-ons like extra storage, phone integrations, or premium support. These costs are real. A practical tip: ask the vendor for a sample invoice for your exact team size and plan before you commit. If they will not provide one, that is a signal. ### Migration Cost Is Usually Underestimated This catches people off guard. Data cleanup, deduplication, fixing formatting in your spreadsheet, field mapping, import testing, and user training all take real time. For a small team, expect 10 to 30 hours of founder or ops lead time on migration alone. If you are moving from another tool, add data export validation and parallel running for 1 to 2 weeks. Budget for this time explicitly. Do not treat it as something you will figure out over a weekend. ### A Simple Total Cost Formula Use this to make your CRM comparison honest: **(Per-user price x number of users x 12 months) + onboarding fees + (estimated migration hours x your hourly value) = Year 1 true cost** Compare this number across your shortlist, not just the sticker price. Getting CRM pricing right at this stage saves you from painful surprises later. ## Step 4: Build a Shortlist and Score Your Candidates You might be tempted to try every CRM that looks promising. Do not. Pick 3 to 5 candidates and evaluate them properly. ### Filter Quickly Using Your Earlier Work Use your must-have list and budget from Steps 2 and 3 to eliminate options fast. Sources for candidates include peer recommendations and review sites like [Capterra](https://www.capterra.com/customer-relationship-management-software/) and [G2](https://www.g2.com/categories/crm), where you can filter by company size. Disqualify anything that does not integrate with the core tools you listed in Step 1. No integration with your email or calendar? It is out. ### Score Each CRM on 5 to 7 Dimensions Set up a simple CRM comparison table. Suggested dimensions: - Fit with your current workflow - Must-have feature coverage - Total Year 1 cost (use the formula from Step 3) - Ease of setup: can you be live in under 2 weeks? - Integration depth with your existing tools - Quality of mobile app - Quality of support and documentation Use a 1-to-5 scale. Have at least one other team member score independently to reduce bias. ### Run a Real Trial Demos are curated. Free trials show you reality. During your trial, do this: import a sample of real data, build your actual pipeline stages, send a few real emails, and test it on mobile. Track how long setup takes and whether you hit friction points. If your team struggles in the trial, they will struggle after purchase. You have a frontrunner. Now the question is: how do you roll this out so your team uses it? ## Step 5: Plan Your Rollout So the CRM Actually Gets Used Choosing the right small business CRM is only half the battle. The other half is getting your team to actually use it. ### Name One Internal CRM Owner This person, often the ops lead or a senior rep, owns data quality, answers questions, and runs onboarding for the first few weeks. Without a clear owner, adoption drifts within the first month. Strong CRM data hygiene starts with someone caring about it from day one. ### Define the Minimum Required Fields Keep it tight. For example: every deal must have a stage, a next step date, and a dollar value. Every contact must have a company and an email. That is it at launch. You can add fields later. You cannot recover from a system people avoid because it feels like paperwork. ### Run a 2-Week Pilot Start with 3 to 5 people. Fix workflow issues and confusing fields before you roll out to the full team. Track simple adoption metrics: are users logging in daily? Are deals moving through stages? Are notes being added after calls? ### Set a Go-Live Date and Retire the Old System Running spreadsheets and a CRM in parallel kills adoption every time. If you can't split billable and non-billable at the point of entry, you create extra work later. - **Retainer and budget tracking.** Can you model a 40-hour monthly retainer and see burn in real time?
